To nag someone means to repeatedly ask, remind, or criticize them about something, usually in a persistent and irritating way. The key idea is repetition — it is not just asking once. It is asking, then asking again, then asking again, and again, until the other person feels annoyed or worn down.

If someone asks you to do the dishes once, that is just asking. But if they bring it up again and again throughout the day — every time they see you, every time you sit down, every time you try to relax — that is nagging.
What Nagging Looks Like in Real Life

Nagging usually happens between two people who are close — a parent and a child, a husband and wife, a boss and an employee. The person who nags is typically frustrated that something is not being done, and they keep pushing, reminding, or complaining to try to make it happen.

For example:

  • A mother keeps telling her teenager to study for the exam. Every evening, she brings it up. Every morning, she brings it up again. The teenager feels suffocated by the constant reminders. The mother is nagging him.
  • A wife keeps reminding her husband to fix the leaking tap. He has been putting it off for two weeks. Every day she mentions it. She is nagging him about it.
  • "Stop nagging me! I will do it when I am ready!" — This is the typical response from a person who is being nagged.

Notice that nagging is not the same as simply reminding. A reminder is neutral and kind. Nagging has a negative quality to it — it is persistent, repetitive, and often done with a tone of frustration, irritation, or complaint. It feels like pressure.

The verb "nag" is used in a few common patterns:

1. Nag + someone

"Please stop nagging me."
"She nags him constantly."
"My boss nags the whole team."

2. Nag + someone + to do something

"She nagged him to clean his room."
"They nagged me to join the club."
"He nagged her to call the doctor."

3. Nag + at + someone

"She kept nagging at him about money."
"He nagged at his children about their manners."

4. Nag + someone + about something

"She nags him about his diet all the time."
"My parents nag me about my future constantly."
The Tone and Feeling Behind Nagging

The word "nag" carries a strongly negative feeling. Calling someone a nag, or saying they are nagging you, means you find their behaviour annoying and excessive. It suggests that the person is not listening the first time, or that the person doing the nagging is being unreasonable, whiny, or relentless.

People rarely describe their own behaviour as nagging. A person who nags usually thinks of themselves as "just reminding" or "caring." But the person on the receiving end feels nagged. This is an important part of the word — it is often used to describe someone else's behaviour, not your own.
The Figurative Use — When Nag Refers to Thoughts, Feelings, and Pain

This is a very important and commonly used meaning of "nag" that you must know. The word is also used to describe something that troubles you persistently in the back of your mind, or a pain that keeps bothering you without going away.

Here, the subject is not a person — it is a thought, a feeling, a doubt, a worry, or a physical pain.

Examples:

"A nagging doubt stayed with him all day." — a doubt that kept coming back, that he could not shake off.

"Something about her answer nagged at him." — he felt something was wrong, and the feeling kept returning, even though he could not explain it.

"A feeling of guilt nagged at her for weeks after the argument." — the guilt was persistent and kept troubling her.

"I have a nagging feeling I forgot something important." — a persistent, uncomfortable sense that something is wrong.

"He has had a nagging pain in his back since the accident." — a dull, persistent pain that does not fully go away.

In all these cases, the idea is the same: something is continuously bothering you, not letting you rest, always coming back. It is like a mental or physical irritation that quietly keeps poking at you.

Because this figurative use is so common, "nagging" is very frequently used as an adjective — placed in front of a noun to describe something persistent and uncomfortable.

Common combinations:

  • A nagging doubt — a doubt that will not leave your mind
  • A nagging feeling — an uncomfortable sense about something
  • A nagging worry — a worry that keeps returning
  • A nagging question — a question you cannot stop thinking about
  • A nagging pain — a dull, continuous pain
  • A nagging cough — a cough that persists and does not go away

You will encounter these combinations very often in reading and conversation, so it is worth knowing them by heart.
How Nag Is Different from Similar Words

• Remind — neutral and helpful; you tell someone something once or gently. No negative feeling.
  • Pester — similar to nag, but pester often implies more of a childlike or minor annoyance. Nagging usually has a more emotional, relationship-based context.
  • Scold — to speak sharply to someone about something wrong they did. It is usually a one-time reaction. Nagging is about repetition, not a single sharp reaction.
  • Criticize — to point out faults. Nagging can include criticism, but it is the repetition that defines nagging.
  • Hound — to relentlessly pursue or pressure someone. More intense than nag, and often used in professional or authoritative contexts.

To nag is to repeatedly and persistently ask, remind, or criticize someone about something, or — when used figuratively — to describe a thought, feeling, or pain that continuously troubles you without giving you peace.
